  <!-- Overview -->
  <div class="overview-grid">
    <div class="z-card">
      <h2 class="overview-heading">🌌 Project Overview</h2>
      <p class="overview-body">
        "Yellowballs" are compact, roughly circular structures in the Milky Way first identified by
        citizen scientists via the Milky Way Project. They are candidate sites of intermediate- to
        high-mass star formation, appearing "yellow" due to the wavelengths they emit most strongly.
        The MIRION catalog (Wolf-Chase et al. 2025) contains 6,176 Yellowballs with photometric
        measurements from the Spitzer and Herschel space telescopes.
      </p>
      <p class="overview-body overview-body--spaced">
        Our team is building a machine learning pipeline to predict <strong>surface mass density
        (SURF_DENS, g/cm²)</strong> — the total gas and dust mass per unit area — from each
        Yellowball's infrared photometric signature. Accurate predictions would allow astronomers
        to characterize newly discovered objects without time-intensive follow-up observations.
      </p>
    </div>

        <p class="stat-value">SURF_DENS (g/cm²)</p>
      </div>

  <!-- Scientific context -->
  <h2 class="section-heading">🔭 Scientific Context</h2>
  <div class="accent-line"></div>
  <div class="z-card card-mb-lg">
    <p class="overview-body">
      Photometry measures how bright an object appears at specific wavelengths of light. Each
      wavelength measurement (called a <em>flux density</em>) is recorded by a telescope filter,
      and together these form a <strong>spectral energy distribution (SED)</strong> — a kind of
      fingerprint encoding information about an object's physical properties like temperature,
      mass, and luminosity.
    </p>
    <p class="overview-body overview-body--spaced">
      Our features come from two telescopes. <strong>Spitzer</strong> provides shorter-wavelength
      bands (8, 12, 24 µm), and <strong>Herschel</strong> provides longer-wavelength bands
      (70, 160, 250, 350, 500, 870, 1100 µm). The 70 µm band is particularly interesting: it
      comes from Herschel but was incorporated directly alongside the Spitzer bands in MIRION,
      and shorter-wavelength bands (including 70 µm) are generally considered more predictive.
    </p>
    <p class="overview-body overview-body--spaced">
      A key research question is: <em>can we make accurate predictions using only the 2–70 µm
      wavelengths?</em> And which specific wavelengths drive the predictions most?
    </p>
  </div>
